categories.name: Emotions & CBT
categories.blurb: Tools for working with thoughts and feelings

models.name: First Principles Thinking
models.tagline: Break a problem down to what is certainly true, then rebuild.

cards.t: Instead of copying how things are usually done, strip a problem back to the facts you know are true and build your answer up from there.

Everyone assumed battery packs had to be expensive. One team priced the raw materials (cobalt, nickel, carbon, aluminium) and found they cost a fraction of the pack price. The real cost was in how packs were made, not what they were made of.
When "that is how it is always done" is the only reason given, when you are stuck, or when costs and rules seem fixed.
Calling an assumption a fact. Test each "fact" by asking how you know it is true.
What do I know for certain, and what am I only assuming because everyone else does?

models.name: Inversion
models.tagline: Solve problems backwards.

cards.t: Instead of asking how to achieve a goal, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things.
Want a great team? List what ruins teams: unclear roles, no feedback, rushed hiring. Remove those first and you are most of the way there.
Planning, risk checks, and any time "be better" advice feels vague.
Stopping at a list of bad outcomes without turning it into specific rules or actions.
What would make this fail for certain, and how do I make sure I never do it?

models.name: Second-Order Thinking
models.tagline: Think past the first consequence.

cards.t: First-order thinking asks what happens next. Second-order thinking asks "and then what?" and follows the consequences several steps out.
Cutting prices boosts sales this month. Then competitors match, margins shrink, and customers expect discounts from now on.
Strategy, policy, habits with delayed effects, and big purchases.
Chasing endless chains of what-ifs. Go two or three steps and focus on the likely ones.
And then what? What happens after that, and after that?

models.name: Occam's Razor
models.tagline: When explanations compete, favour the one that needs the fewest assumptions.

cards.t: If two explanations fit the facts equally well, the simpler one is usually the better place to start.
Website traffic drops overnight. The simplest explanation is a tracking or deployment error, not a secret search penalty plus a rival's plot.
Debugging, diagnosing problems, and weighing competing theories.
Treating "simple" as always right. It is a tiebreaker between explanations that fit equally well, not proof.
Which explanation needs the fewest things to be true?

models.name: Hanlon's Razor
models.tagline: Do not blame malice for what carelessness can explain.

cards.t: Before assuming someone meant harm, consider that they were rushed, distracted or did not know.
A colleague leaves you off an email. They most likely forgot or were in a hurry, not shutting you out.
Conflict, ambiguous messages and online disagreements.
Using it to excuse genuine repeated harm. If a pattern keeps going, it is no longer an accident.
What is the most ordinary, innocent reason for this?

models.name: Map vs Territory
models.tagline: The model is not the thing it describes.

cards.t: Every map, plan, metric or forecast is a simplified picture of reality. It is useful, but it leaves things out, and when the two disagree, reality wins.
A project tracker says the work is 90 percent done, but nobody has tried it with a real customer.
Trusting dashboards, KPIs, org charts, plans and forecasts.
Optimising the map: hitting the metric while the real goal drifts away.
What does my map leave out, and when did I last check the real thing?

models.name: Circle of Competence
models.tagline: Know where your knowledge is solid and where it ends.

cards.t: Everyone has areas they understand deeply. Good decisions come from staying inside that circle, or knowing precisely where its edge is.
A skilled chef judging the economics of a restaurant is inside their circle. The same chef buying biotech shares on a tip is well outside it.
Investing, hiring, giving advice and taking on new projects.
Never growing the circle. Expand it deliberately by learning, not by guessing.
Do I understand this well enough to explain how it could go wrong?

models.name: Bayesian Thinking
models.tagline: Update your beliefs as evidence arrives.

cards.t: Start with a best guess based on what you already know. When new evidence appears, adjust the belief in proportion to how strong the evidence is. Beliefs come in degrees, not yes or no.
You think a start-up has a 10 percent chance of succeeding. A major customer signs. You raise your estimate, but not to 100 percent.
Forecasting, hiring, interpreting test results and any uncertain call.
Ignoring how common something is to begin with, or swinging wildly on one piece of evidence.
How likely did I think this was before, and how much should this new evidence really change that?

models.name: Steel-Manning
models.tagline: Argue against the strongest version of the other side.

cards.t: The opposite of a straw man. Restate the other view in its best, most convincing form before you respond to it.
Before rejecting a rival's proposal, describe it so well that its supporters would say "yes, exactly".
Disagreements, big decisions, writing and negotiations.
Doing it as a trick to win. The aim is to understand, and you may change your mind.
Could I state their view so well that they would agree with my version?

models.name: Dichotomy of Control
models.tagline: Sort what is up to you from what is not.

cards.t: A Stoic idea. Some things are in your control: your judgements, choices and effort. Others are not: outcomes, other people's opinions, the weather. Spend your energy on the first group.
You cannot control whether you get the job. You can control your preparation, your answers and how you handle the result.
Anxiety, setbacks, waiting for results and workplace frustration.
Writing things off as outside your control when you can partly influence them. Focus on your part.
What part of this is truly mine to decide or do?

models.name: Chesterton's Fence
models.tagline: Do not remove a fence until you know why it was built.

cards.t: Before you scrap a rule, process or tradition that looks pointless, find out why it exists.
A strange approval step in a process looks useless. Before deleting it, find out what problem it was added to prevent.
Changing rules, code, processes and inherited systems.
Using it to defend everything old. Once you know the reason, you can still remove the fence.
Do I know why this exists?

models.name: Opportunity Cost
models.tagline: Every choice has a hidden price: the best option you gave up.

cards.t: The true cost of anything is what you could have done with the same time or money instead.
A 500 pound gadget is not just 500 pounds. It is also the trip, course or savings you did not choose. An evening of scrolling costs you whatever else you would have done with it.
Spending time or money, saying yes to requests and career moves.
Counting only money. Time and attention are often the biggest costs.
What is the next best use of this time or money?

models.name: Regret Minimization Framework
models.tagline: Picture yourself at 80, looking back.

cards.t: For big life choices, imagine you are very old and ask which choice you would regret not having made.
A well-known founder used it when deciding whether to leave a secure job to start a company. At 80, he figured he would regret not trying far more than trying and failing.
Big, hard-to-reverse choices about career, moving and relationships.
Letting it justify reckless moves. Pair it with a realistic look at the risks.
At 80, which choice will I regret not having made?

models.name: Eisenhower Matrix
models.tagline: Sort tasks by urgent versus important.

cards.t: Four boxes: urgent and important (do now), important but not urgent (schedule), urgent but not important (delegate), and neither (drop).
A client emergency is do now. Planning next quarter is schedule. Most emails can be delegated or dropped.
An overloaded week, planning and prioritising.
Living in "urgent". The important-but-not-urgent box is where growth happens, so protect time for it.
Is this important, urgent, both, or neither?

models.name: Margin of Safety
models.tagline: Build in a buffer for what you cannot predict.

cards.t: Plan so that you are fine even if you are quite wrong. The buffer is what protects you from surprises.
An engineer designs a bridge to hold many times its expected load. A traveller leaves for the airport an hour earlier than the map suggests.
Investing, budgeting, deadlines and anything fragile.
Sizing the buffer from the best case. Base it on how wrong you could be.
If I am wrong by a lot, will I still be okay?

models.name: Pre-Mortem
models.tagline: Imagine the project has failed, then explain why.

cards.t: Before you start, picture that it has already failed, and write down the reasons. It is easier to spot risks when failure feels real.
Before a launch, the team imagines it flopped in six months and lists causes: no demand testing, a key person leaves, bad timing. Then they fix those now.
Before launching, hiring or making big commitments.
Listing only vague causes like "poor execution". Be specific enough to act on.
It is a year from now and this failed. What went wrong?

models.name: Expected Value
models.tagline: Weigh each outcome by how likely it is.

cards.t: Multiply each possible outcome by its probability and add them up. It tells you what a gamble is worth on average.
A 10 percent chance to win 1,000 pounds is worth 100 pounds on average. A sure 80 pounds is worth less in expectation, though you may still prefer certainty.
Bets, investments, negotiations and product choices.
Ignoring the size of the downside. A small chance of ruin can outweigh a good average.
What are the outcomes, how likely is each, and can I survive the worst one?

models.name: One-Way and Two-Way Doors
models.tagline: Decide fast when you can undo it, slowly when you cannot.

cards.t: Two-way doors can be walked back through if you do not like what you find. One-way doors cannot. Treat them differently.
Trying a new tool for a week is a two-way door. Signing a five-year lease is a one-way door.
Product decisions, hiring, purchases and team speed.
Treating every decision as a one-way door. It slows everything down.
If this turns out to be wrong, can I go back, and what would it cost?

models.name: Pareto Principle (80/20)
models.tagline: Roughly 80 percent of results come from 20 percent of causes.

cards.t: Results are rarely spread evenly. A small share of inputs usually drives most of the output.
A handful of customers produce most of the revenue, and a few tasks create most of your impact.
Prioritising, managing time and cutting scope.
Taking 80/20 as an exact rule. The point is that it is uneven, so find the vital few.
Which few things are driving most of the results?

models.name: Compounding
models.tagline: Small gains that build on themselves grow explosively.

cards.t: When each gain is added to the base that produces the next one, growth curves upward instead of rising in a straight line.
Improving by 1 percent a day for a year leaves you about 38 times better. Savings earn interest on their interest.
Habits, learning, investing and reputation.
Quitting early. The curve looks flat at the start, and most of the growth comes later.
What small thing could I repeat so consistently that it compounds?

models.name: Feedback Loops
models.tagline: Outputs feed back in as inputs.

cards.t: Reinforcing loops amplify a change (more users bring more content, which brings more users). Balancing loops steady it (a thermostat turns the heating off when the room warms).
Success attracts talent, which creates more success. A thermostat keeps a room at the same temperature.
Understanding growth, spirals, habits and systems that surprise you.
Expecting straight lines. Look for delays, because they cause overshoot.
What is this result feeding back into?

models.name: Leverage
models.tagline: Multiply your effort with tools, people, money or code.

cards.t: Leverage lets a small input produce a large output.
Writing a book once can reach thousands of people. A short script can save hours every week.
Scaling your work, careers and businesses.
Forgetting that leverage amplifies mistakes as well as wins.
What could do this work for me, or make one hour count for ten?

models.name: Bottlenecks
models.tagline: A system moves only as fast as its slowest step.

cards.t: Also called the Theory of Constraints. Improving anything except the constraint changes nothing about the overall result.
A restaurant with fast chefs but one till has long queues. Speeding up the kitchen does not help. Fix the till.
Slow processes, teams and personal workflows.
Improving steps that are not the constraint.
What is the one step holding everything else back?

models.name: Network Effects
models.tagline: A product gets more valuable as more people use it.

cards.t: Each new user makes the whole thing better for the existing ones, which attracts more users.
A messaging app is useless on your own and valuable once your friends are on it.
Platforms, marketplaces and communities.
Assuming growth alone creates one. Early users need value before the network is big.
Does each new user make this better for the others?

models.name: Diminishing Returns
models.tagline: Each extra unit of effort adds less than the last.

cards.t: Past a certain point, more input produces smaller and smaller gains.
The first hour of revision helps a lot, the tenth hardly at all. The first coffee wakes you up, the fifth does not.
Studying, optimising, spending and perfectionism.
Stopping too early, before the useful part. Know where the curve flattens.
Is the next hour, or the next pound, still earning its place?

models.name: Confirmation Bias
models.tagline: We favour information that agrees with what we already believe.

cards.t: Once we hold a view, we notice supporting evidence and quietly skip or dismiss the rest.
After deciding a diet works, you notice every success story and skip the studies that say otherwise.
Research, hiring, investing and arguments.
Thinking you are immune. Everyone does it, so build in checks.
What evidence would change my mind, and have I looked for it?

models.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
models.tagline: People with little skill often cannot see their own gaps.

cards.t: In unfamiliar areas we may not know enough to judge how much we do not know. The popular "mountain" graph is a simplification, but the core idea is real.
After a week learning a language you feel fluent, until you meet a native speaker.
Learning new skills, giving feedback and hiring.
Using it to label other people as foolish. It applies to all of us in areas we do not know well.
What might I not know that I do not know?

models.name: Hedonic Adaptation
models.tagline: We get used to good (and bad) changes.

cards.t: Our happiness tends to drift back to a baseline after a change, even a big one.
A raise or a new car feels great, then becomes normal within months.
Purchases, career goals, relationships and gratitude.
Chasing the next upgrade expecting lasting happiness. Experiences and variety fade less.
Will this still feel special in six months?

models.name: Anchoring
models.tagline: The first number you see pulls your judgement toward it.

cards.t: An early number, even an irrelevant one, becomes a reference point that later estimates cling to.
A jacket marked "was 300, now 150" feels like a bargain, even if it is only worth 80.
Negotiating, shopping, salary talks and estimating.
Thinking that awareness is enough. Research your own number first.
Where did my first number come from?

models.name: Survivorship Bias
models.tagline: We only see the winners.

cards.t: We study the successes that are visible and forget the many failures that vanished, so we draw the wrong lessons.

Stories of famous dropouts hide the many who did not make it. In the Second World War, analysts wanted to armour the parts of returning planes that had bullet holes, until Abraham Wald pointed out that the planes hit elsewhere never came back.
Business advice, success stories, investing and case studies.
Studying only the winners and calling their shared traits the cause.
What happened to the ones I am not seeing?

models.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
models.tagline: Money already spent should not decide what you do next.

cards.t: Past costs that cannot be recovered are irrelevant to the choice in front of you, but they still feel important.
You keep going to a gym you hate, or keep funding a failing project, because you have already paid so much.
Projects, subscriptions, investments and long commitments.
Confusing it with commitment. Persistence is fine when future benefits justify it, not when past costs do.
If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?

models.name: Incentives
models.tagline: People respond to what is rewarded.

cards.t: Behaviour follows incentives, often more than it follows intentions or instructions.
Pay sales staff on volume and they discount heavily. Pay on profit and their behaviour changes.
Designing teams, pricing and policy, and understanding odd behaviour.
Assuming bad intent when the incentive explains it. You get what you reward.
What is this person rewarded or punished for?

models.name: Social Proof
models.tagline: We copy what other people do.

cards.t: When unsure, we look to others for clues about what is right or good.
A busy restaurant looks better than an empty one. Reviews and "most popular" labels work the same way.
Marketing, habits and group decisions.
Following the crowd when the crowd is guessing too.
Do I actually like this, or does everyone else?

models.name: Principle of Charity
models.tagline: Read people in the most reasonable way.

cards.t: When someone's words could mean several things, assume the sensible, good-faith meaning first.
A blunt message from a colleague: assume hurry, not rudeness, and reply to the best reading.
Disagreements, reading messages and debates.
Being naive about clear bad faith.
What is the most sensible reading of what they said?

models.name: The Thoughts, Feelings and Behaviour Cycle
models.tagline: How you read a situation shapes how you feel and what you do.

cards.t: A core idea in CBT. It is often our interpretation of a situation, not the situation itself, that drives our feelings and actions. Change the thought or the behaviour and the whole cycle shifts.
Your manager asks for a quick chat. Read as "I am in trouble", it brings anxiety and avoidance. Read as "maybe they want my input", it brings curiosity.
Noticing a spiral, or working out why you reacted the way you did.
Thinking it means "just think positive". The aim is realistic, balanced thinking.
What did I tell myself about what happened?

flow.t: Your manager asks for a quick chat.
Avoids eye contact, rehearses worst cases.

models.name: Cognitive Distortions
models.tagline: Habitual thinking traps that twist how we read events.

cards.t: Common patterns include all-or-nothing thinking, mind-reading, catastrophising, "should" statements and emotional reasoning ("I feel like a failure, so I must be one").
A friend does not reply to your message. Mind-reading says "they are annoyed with me". A fairer reading is that they are busy.
When a thought feels certain but harsh, or after an argument.
Labelling every thought a distortion. Some worries are accurate.
Which thinking trap might be at work, and what is the evidence for and against?

models.name: Cognitive Reframing
models.tagline: Find a more balanced way to see it.

cards.t: Reframing replaces an unhelpful thought with one that is just as true, but fairer and more useful.
"I messed up the presentation, I am hopeless" becomes "One section went badly, the rest went fine, and I know what to practise."
After setbacks, during anxiety and when you are being self-critical.
Forcing false positivity. A good reframe is believable.
What would I say to a friend in this situation?

flow.t: One part went badly. Others went well.
"I made a mistake and can improve."

models.name: Catastrophizing
models.tagline: Jumping to the worst possible outcome.

cards.t: A small problem is treated as the start of a disaster. Rating how likely the worst case really is can bring it back to size.
A small error in a report becomes "I will be fired and lose my home". Ask: what is the worst case, the best case, the most likely case, and how would I cope?
Worry spirals and the lead-up to big events.
Dismissing real risks. Aim for realistic, not rosy.
What is the worst, the best and the most likely outcome, and how would I cope?

models.name: Thought Record
models.tagline: Write the thought down and test it.

cards.t: A simple CBT worksheet: situation, automatic thought, emotion, evidence for, evidence against, and a balanced thought.
Situation: no reply to an invitation. Thought: "Nobody wants me there." Evidence against: two friends already said yes. Balanced thought: "People are busy."
Repeating worries and strong emotions.
Doing it only in your head. Writing slows the thought down enough to examine it.
What is the evidence for and against this thought?

models.name: Behavioural Activation
models.tagline: Action first, motivation follows.

cards.t: Low mood makes everything feel pointless, so you do less, which lowers mood further. Scheduling small, doable activities that matter to you can break the loop.
Choose one small, valued action, like a ten-minute walk, and notice how you feel afterwards.
Low mood, procrastination and feeling stuck.
Waiting to feel like it. Start tiny. If low mood lasts, talk to a professional.
What is one small thing I could do today that matters to me?
